Hermes. The Olympian god of messages, boundaries, commerce, thieves, and the dead in Greek mythology. Born of Zeus and the nymph Maia, Hermes is characteristically clever, quick-witted, and amoral, equally comfortable aiding heroes as deceiving them. As divine messenger, he guides souls to the Underworld. As protector of travelers and merchants, he represents boundaries, transitions, and the movement of goods and information. His attribute is the caduceus, the staff entwined with serpents.

He is the son of Zeus and the Pleiad nymph Maia, born in a secret cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia. Known for precocious cleverness from birth, he stole cattle from Apollo on his first day alive. He invented the lyre on the day of his birth from a tortoise shell, creating music so enchanting that Apollo was moved to forgive the cattle theft and trade him the caduceus for the instrument in return.

He serves as the divine messenger between gods and mortals, traveling between Olympus and the mortal realm. He also functions as psychopompos, the guide of souls to the Underworld and Hades. He wears the petasos, a winged hat, and the winged sandals called talaria, symbols of his speed and mobility. He carries the caduceus, the herald's staff around which two serpents are entwined, later a medical symbol.

He delivered the sealed jar containing human sorrows to Pandora before her marriage to Epimetheus, making him instrumental in humanity's suffering and the fall of the Golden Age. He provided crucial aid to Perseus, gifting him the adamantine, unbreakable sickle and winged sandals essential for beheading Medusa while invisible via Athena's helm of darkness.

Characterized as both helpful and mischievous, he serves as patron of thieves, merchants, travelers, speakers, and heralds, blurring the line between trickery and legitimate commerce, theft and cleverness. He presides over boundaries, transitions, commerce, language, persuasion, and journeys. His domain encompasses all crossroads, where herms, stone pillars, marked his presence, and all liminal spaces.

Zeus is his father and the king of the gods who sends him on missions. Hades is the god of the Underworld whom Hermes frequently encounters as a psychopomp. Pandora is the figure whose deception he facilitated by delivering her to humanity. Perseus is the hero whom he assisted in his quest against Medusa. Apollo is his rival and eventual ally, with whom he had conflict over the lyre. Merchants and commerce are the domain over which he presides as protector.
